narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Ōte'a predates European contact in Tahiti, where it was initially a male-only war dance.
Its modern form was established during the latter half of the 20th century, largely influenced by the competitive requirements of the Heiva i Tahiti festival.
on_screen: Map: French Polynesia · Oceania
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed at festivals like the Heiva i Tahiti, as well as at luaus and international Polynesian dance recitals.
It serves as a narrative medium, with gestures often depicting daily life, warfare, or nature.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features rapid, synchronized hip-shaking.
Men perform scissor-like leg movements, while women focus on hip-swaying.
Choreography involves specific figures such as tamau, varu, otamu, ami, and fa'arapu, with arm and hand gestures that remain consistent across the group.
Watch for tamau, varu, fa'arapu.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (2QahgraRrYs)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers in several rows
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music consists exclusively of percussion, specifically the tōʻere (slit log drum), pahu (shark-skin drum), and faʻatētē.
There is no singing or melodic instrumentation.
Listen for the tōʻere, pahu, faʻatētē.

The music is defined by the sharp, hollow resonance of the tōʻere slit drums, the deeper thud of the pahu, and the rapid, driving beat of the faʻatētē, creating a complex, purely percussive soundscape.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Teuira Henry (documented the dance in 1928) and Patrick O'Reilly (author of 'La danse à Tahiti').
Variations exist between the traditional Tahitian practice and the modern, tourist-oriented interpretations found in the Hawaiian Islands and other Pacific-rim resorts.
The Ōte'a is a form of 'ori tahiti.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Ōte'a is sibling of aparima: Aparima involves singing, whereas Ōte'a is purely percussion.
Ōte'a is sibling of tāmūrē: Tāmūrē is a couple's dance that incorporates steps from the Ōte'a.
